_doc: Director-safe component palette. The AI director chooses from these. Each entry: when to use AND when not to, concrete APUSH examples, hard constraints enforced by the pipeline validator, and per-prop type/required/example.

constraints: props.title is required and must be non-empty (validator rejects empty titles).
Keep title under ~40 characters; kicker under ~20. Long titles overflow the card.
Use at most 3-4 title scenes per episode (open + act breaks). More than that feels like a slideshow, not a lesson.
examples: Episode open: title 'The Bill Comes Due', kicker 'U3E1', subline 'War debt, the Proclamation Line, and Pontiac's Rebellion'
Act break: title 'Box Two', kicker 'The Proclamation Line of 1763', subline 'London draws a fence it cannot patrol'
components.name: title

subline.example: War debt, the Proclamation Line, and Pontiac's Rebellion

components.when: Use for the episode open, act breaks, and major topic shifts — moments where the narration itself announces a new section. Do NOT use for ordinary exposition beats or mid-argument transitions; a title card that says nothing new wastes a scene and breaks pacing.

constraints: props.image is required and MUST be an exact key from AVAILABLE IMAGES (see image_rules). Never invent a path.
Validator rejects image paths starting with http:, https:, data:, blob:, or / — and any path containing '..'. Use the registry key as-is.
stops is optional; if provided it must be exactly [[x,y,scale],[x,y,scale]] with x,y in 0..1 and scale >= 1.0. Omit it to use the default slow zoom.
examples: Grenville portrait while Marcus explains 'his math was brutally simple' — image historic/u3e1/george-grenville-portrait.jpg, caption 'Prime minister, 1763-1765'
Proclamation map while Maya says 'a line along the crest' — image historic/u3e1/proclamation-line-map.jpg, caption 'No settlement past the Appalachians'
components.name: ken_burns

caption.example: Prime minister, 1763-1765. Author of the Stamp Act.

components.when: The default scene for most beats: one historic image with a slow zoom/pan while the hosts narrate. Use whenever the narration describes a person, place, document, or event that has a matching image. Do NOT use when the narration is making an abstract argument with no visual anchor — use highlight or compare instead. Do NOT use two ken_burns scenes back-to-back on the same image; vary the visual.

constraints: props.quote is required and must be non-empty.
Never fabricate a historical quote. If the script says a promise is paraphrased, do not present it as a quote.
Keep quotes under ~140 characters so they fit the card at 1280x720.
examples: Maya's landing line as a quote card: quote 'Cheap beats fair when the treasury's empty.'
Marcus's thesis: quote 'Britain won the war, and wrecked the arrangement that had made the empire work.'
components.name: quote

quote.example: Britain won the war, and wrecked the arrangement that had made the empire work.

components.when: Use for a genuine quotation — a line actually spoken in the episode that deserves to land on screen, or a verbatim historical quote from a document. Do NOT use for paraphrases or your own summary sentences; a quote card implies 'someone said exactly this.' If the narration paraphrases (e.g., 'the Proclamation's Native-land promise is paraphrased, not quoted'), use ken_burns with a caption instead.

constraints: Both props.left and props.right are required objects (validator rejects the scene if either is missing).
Each side: {head: string, sections: [{sub: string, points: string[]}]}. Keep each side to 1-2 sections with 2-4 short points each — more overflows the card.
Keep point strings under ~60 characters each.
examples: British vs Colonial view of war debt: left head 'London's ledger' (points: colonies benefited most, paid least, taxes a fraction of England's), right head 'The colonial ledger' (points: sent their sons, fulfilled their obligation, a bill with no vote is a shakedown)

French vs British Native diplomacy: left head 'The French way' (negotiated, ceremonies, gift-giving as dominance and protection), right head 'Amherst's way' (gifts demeaning, cut off, soldiers and settlers)
components.name: compare

left.example: {"head": "London's ledger", "sections": [{"sub": "The case", "points": ["Colonies gained the most", "Paid the least"]}]}

right.example: {"head": "The colonial ledger", "sections": [{"sub": "The counter", "points": ["Sent their sons", "No vote, no tax"]}]}

components.when: Use when the narration sets two things side by side: British vs colonial views, before vs after, French vs British approaches. The classic trigger is a 'both sides' or 'two ledgers' beat. Do NOT use for a simple list or a single-sided explanation — that's highlight. Do NOT use when there are three or more sides; use causal_chain or separate scenes.

constraints: props.nodes must be an array of 2 to 5 strings (validator rejects 1 or 6+).
Each node under ~70 characters. Nodes render as linked steps; long nodes overflow.
Order nodes strictly cause → effect. The last node is the consequence the narration lands on.
examples: War debt → Grenville's math → end of salutary neglect: nodes ['Seven Years' War leaves London drowning in debt', 'Grenville: colonies benefited most, paid least', 'London starts enforcing the trade laws it ignored for a century']
Amherst ends gift-giving → Pontiac organizes → forts fall: nodes ['Amherst cuts the gift ceremonies', 'Pontiac organizes the resistance, 1763', 'Fort after fort falls around the Great Lakes']
components.name: causal_chain

nodes.example: ["War leaves London drowning in debt", "Grenville taxes the colonies", "Salutary neglect ends"]

components.when: Use for cause → effect sequences where each step leads to the next: war debt leads to taxes, taxes lead to resistance. The narration trigger is usually 'so', 'which meant', 'and that led to'. Do NOT use for a mere chronological list with no causal links — that's timeline. Do NOT use for two-sided arguments — that's compare.

constraints: props.body is required and non-empty; props.highlights must be a non-empty array (validator rejects empty).
Each highlight: {text: string (required), note: string (optional)}. The text should appear in or closely match the body.
Use for 1-3 highlights per scene. More than 3 clutters the RedPen annotations.
examples: Key term 'salutary neglect': body 'For a hundred years, London barely enforced its own trade laws...', highlights [{text: 'salutary neglect', note: 'Beneficial neglect — Burke coined the name in 1775'}]

Key term 'Proclamation Line of 1763': body 'A line along the crest of the Appalachians, and no colonial settlement past it.', highlights [{text: 'Appalachians', note: 'The fence — not the Mississippi, which was the prize'}]
components.name: highlight

body.example: For a hundred years, London barely enforced its own trade laws: absentee customs officers, smuggled molasses.

components.when: Use for key terms and exam concepts: the moment the narration defines a term the student must know. The trigger is usually 'the books call it X' or a definition beat. Do NOT use for general exposition — that's ken_burns. Do NOT use when the term is just mentioned in passing without being defined.

constraints: All six props are required and non-empty: documentTitle, authorAndDate, excerptText, highlightedPhrase, hippType, hippExplanation.
props.highlightedPhrase MUST appear verbatim (exact substring) in props.excerptText — the validator rejects the scene otherwise, because the highlight would render nothing.
props.hippType must be one of H, I, P, P (Historical context, Intended audience, Purpose, Point of view).
Never invent document language. If the script paraphrases, do not use this component.
examples: Royal Proclamation of 1763: documentTitle 'The Royal Proclamation of 1763', authorAndDate 'King George III, October 1763', excerptText with the actual proclamation language, highlightedPhrase a verbatim phrase from the excerpt, hippType 'P', hippExplanation 'London was dodging another expensive frontier war — purpose before grievance.'
Sugar Act (1764): documentTitle 'The Sugar Act', authorAndDate 'Parliament, 1764', excerptText from the act, hippType 'H'
components.name: primary_source

excerptText.example: ...that no Governor... presume... to grant warrants of survey... beyond the heads or sources of any of the rivers which fall into the Atlantic Ocean...

highlightedPhrase.example: beyond the heads or sources of any of the rivers which fall into the Atlantic Ocean

hippExplanation.example: London was dodging another expensive frontier war. Purpose before grievance — that is how these sources crack open.

components.when: Use for document analysis beats — the HIPP moments (Historical context, Intended audience, Purpose, Point of view). The trigger is the narration dissecting a document: a proclamation, an act, a letter. Do NOT use for paraphrased content; this component presents an excerpt as a real document, so excerptText must be genuine document language. Do NOT use more than twice per episode — it is the heaviest cognitive lift.

constraints: props.speaker must be exactly 'maya' or 'marcus' (lowercase, validator rejects anything else).
props.image is optional; if provided it must be an exact AVAILABLE IMAGES key (see image_rules).
Use talking_head for roughly 1 in 4-5 scenes so the hosts stay present without crowding out the history.
examples: Maya's exam tip: speaker 'maya' — 'If a stimulus hands you the Proclamation's promise, ask what the source is for. Purpose before the grievance.'
Marcus's thesis: speaker 'marcus' — 'Britain won the war, and wrecked the arrangement that had made the empire work.'
components.name: talking_head
components.when: Use for direct host presence: exam tips ('Tip for the test...'), thesis statements, banter, and prediction beats. The user expects talking heads in video lessons — a graphics-only episode feels incomplete. Use when the narration is Maya or Marcus speaking AS themselves (advice, asides, humor) rather than narrating history. Do NOT use for straight historical narration — that's ken_burns.

constraints: props.events must be a non-empty array (validator rejects empty).
Each event: {date: string, label: string}. Keep labels under ~50 characters.
Order events chronologically. 3-6 events per scene is the sweet spot.
examples: Postwar escalation: events [{date: '1763', label: 'Proclamation Line drawn'}, {date: '1764', label: 'Sugar Act'}, {date: '1765', label: 'Stamp Act'}]
Pontiac's Rebellion: events [{date: '1760-61', label: "Neolin's vision"}, {date: '1763', label: 'Pontiac organizes'}, {date: 'Aug 1763', label: 'Gage replaces Amherst'}]
components.name: timeline
components.when: Use for chronological sequences where the ORDER of events is the point: 1763 → 1764 → 1765 (Proclamation, Sugar Act, Stamp Act). Do NOT use when the events are causally linked step-by-step — that's causal_chain. Do NOT use for two-sided comparisons — that's compare.

constraints: props.title is required (validator rejects empty).
props.highlights should be place names from places.json (e.g., 'Appalachian Mountains', 'Great Lakes', 'Fort Detroit'). Unknown names may not resolve on the map.
Name only places the narration actually mentions. Highlighting unmentioned places confuses the student.
examples: Proclamation Line: title 'The Proclamation Line, 1763', highlights ['Appalachian Mountains'] — while Maya explains 'a line along the crest'
Pontiac's Rebellion: title 'The forts fall, 1763', highlights ['Fort Detroit', 'Great Lakes']
components.name: map
components.when: Use when geography IS the argument: the Proclamation Line along the Appalachians, Pontiac's forts around the Great Lakes, the 'fence vs prize' distinction (Appalachians = fence, Mississippi = prize). Do NOT use for a decorative backdrop — if the narration doesn't name places, use ken_burns instead.

constraints: Both props.left and props.right are required objects (validator rejects the scene if either is missing).
Each side: {name: string, subtitle?: string, points: string[]}. Keep 2-4 points per side, each under ~60 characters.
Name the camps, don't just label them 'Side A / Side B'.
examples: Was the Proclamation punishment or triage? left {name: 'The colonial read', points: ['Britain is punishing us', 'No Ohio for you']}, right {name: 'London's reality', points: ['Terrified of a second war', 'Triage, not revenge']}
Neolin vs Pontiac roles: left {name: 'Neolin', points: ['The prophet', '1760-61 vision']}, right {name: 'Pontiac', points: ['The war chief', '1763 organizer']}
components.name: versus
components.when: Use for a debate or clash of interpretations — stronger than compare. Where compare lays two views side by side neutrally, versus frames them as opposing camps with named positions. The trigger is narration like 'historians disagree' or a direct contradiction. Do NOT use for neutral before/after — that's compare.

constraints: props.images must be an array of 2 to 4 image paths (validator rejects fewer than 2).
Every path MUST be an exact key from AVAILABLE IMAGES (see image_rules). One invented filename breaks the whole collage.
All images should be the same orientation family (all portraits or all landscapes) for a clean grid.
examples: The men of 1763: images [george-grenville-portrait.jpg, edmund-burke.jpg] with title 'The men who redrew the empire'
Forts under siege: images [fort-detroit-siege.jpg, fort-pitt-plan.jpg] with title 'The forts fall'
components.name: collage

title.example: The men who redrew the empire

components.when: Use when the narration names several people or things in quick succession and no single image carries the beat: a run of portraits (Grenville, Burke, Amherst, Gage) or a set of related artifacts. Do NOT use for a single subject — that's ken_burns. Do NOT use more than 4 images; the tiles get too small to read at 1280x720.

image_rules._doc: Image paths are the #1 source of broken renders. Follow these exactly.
rules: Copy image paths EXACTLY from AVAILABLE IMAGES. Never modify, abbreviate, expand, or reconstruct filenames.
If unsure which image fits, use ken_burns with the closest matching image. Do not invent a filename that 'sounds right'.
Every image value must be a key that appears verbatim in the AVAILABLE IMAGES list sent with this prompt.

wrong_vs_right.why_wrong: Invented filename. The registry key is edmund-burke.jpg. Adding '-portrait' breaks the render.
Reconstructed from the description. The registry key is proclamation-line-map.jpg.
"grenville.jpg" is abbreviated; the key is george-grenville-portrait.jpg. Copy, don't shorten.
